title: Raines v. Byrd
lead: Six lawmakers sue immediately after the line-item cancellation law takes effect, but their lost political power does not provide the personal injury needed to decide the law’s constitutionality.

actors.name: Four Senators and two House members
actors.role: Legislators who voted against the Line Item Veto Act and challenged it.

actors.name: President Bill Clinton
actors.role: Signed the Act assigning presidential cancellation authority.

actors.name: Treasury Secretary and OMB Director
actors.role: Executive defendants defending against the constitutional suit.

proceedings: The District of Columbia district court found standing and ripeness and declared the Act unconstitutional on summary judgment.
Executive officials appealed directly under the statute.
The Supreme Court vacated and remanded for dismissal for lack of jurisdiction, 7–2, without reaching constitutionality.
limits: The majority had six votes; Ginsburg also joined Souter’s judgment concurrence. Coleman involved decisive votes against ratification. The Court did not foreclose every institutional plaintiff or a later personally injured challenger.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Congress enacts cancellation authority over specified spending and tax benefits
sections.cue: What changed after a President signed legislation?
paragraphs: The Senate passed the Line Item Veto Act 69–31 on March 27, 1996, and the House passed the identical bill 232–177 the next day. President Clinton signed April 4, with effect January 1, 1997. It permitted cancellation after signing of specified discretionary budget authority, new direct spending, or limited tax benefits upon determinations of deficit reduction, no impairment of essential functions, and no national-interest harm. A timely special message went to Congress.

Congress could nullify cancellation through a disapproval bill, but that bill required ordinary presentment and faced presidential veto. Four Senators and two House members who had voted against the Act sued the Treasury Secretary and Office of Management and Budget Director on January 2, 1997. One, Senator Hatfield, had retired with the prior Congress.

They claimed future votes would change meaning: a signed package no longer assured its whole effect, repeal could occur without their legislative participation, and power shifted to the Executive. The Act expressly allowed congressional members and adversely affected individuals to bring an expedited District of Columbia challenge. The district court found standing and ripeness before any cancellation and granted summary judgment invalidating the Act under the Presentment Clause and nondelegation principles. The Executive officials appealed directly, contesting standing and ripeness.

sources.pinpoint: Act and lawsuit; 521 U.S. 814–818 & n.1, 825 n.9

sections.title: Rehnquist asks whether these plaintiffs suffered a judicially cognizable injury
sections.cue: Why did Congress’s invitation to sue not settle Article III?
paragraphs: On direct appeal Chief Justice Rehnquist addressed standing first. Personal, particularized, concrete injury, traceability, and likely redress were necessary, with special rigor when judging another branch’s constitutionality. Statutory permission could remove prudential obstacles and lessen concern about unwanted congressional conflict, but could not supply missing constitutional injury.

The alleged loss was political power shared by legislative officeholders, not deprivation of these individuals’ seats, salaries, or private rights. Powell v. McCormack involved exclusion from an elected seat and its salary, a personal entitlement. Raines’s plaintiffs instead complained of the office’s institutional influence. Desire for prompt adjudication of an important dispute was insufficient.

sources.pinpoint: Standing and claimed injury; 521 U.S. 818–821 & n.3

sections.title: The lawmakers lost a vote rather than having decisive votes nullified
sections.cue: How did the Court distinguish Coleman?
paragraphs: In Coleman v. Miller, twenty Kansas Senators voted against amendment ratification and claimed an unauthorized lieutenant-governor tie vote nullified their otherwise decisive opposition. Rehnquist read that case at most to protect legislators whose sufficient votes to pass or defeat a specific measure were completely nullified. Its historical standing majority included some merits dissenters, so the two alignments differed.

These federal plaintiffs’ anti-Act votes were fully counted. They lost, received no lesser weight, and could still gather enough colleagues to reject appropriations, repeal the Act, or exempt particular laws. Changed future effectiveness differed from complete nullification. The Court reserved additional distinctions involving Coleman’s state legislators and state-court origin.

History reinforced restraint: conflicts over removal, appointments, legislative and pocket vetoes did not usually produce immediate suits alleging reduced institutional power. Review instead came through traditional injuries, such as the salary claim in Myers. Other systems might allow direct institutional litigation, but Article III practice had been narrower.

sections.title: Political remedies and later injured parties remain available
sections.cue: What did the judgment decide and what did the separate opinions prefer?
paragraphs: The plaintiffs lacked authorization to represent either House. Congressional amici opposed the merits while taking no standing position; institutional opposition was relevant, not an independent jurisdiction test. Political remedies remained, and someone personally harmed by cancellation could sue later. The Court also questioned whether injury traced to the Executive defendants rather than legislators who enacted the law, while reserving different circumstances.

On June 26, 1997, the Court vacated the constitutional judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction. Rehnquist’s opinion included O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, and Ginsburg—six votes. Souter supplied a seventh judgment vote in a concurrence also joined by Ginsburg. He found personal-versus-official and abstract-versus-concrete distinctions debatable but considered separation of powers decisive here. Awaiting a private beneficiary deprived of funds would distance courts from both interbranch and intracongressional conflict without excluding all official injury.

Stevens dissented, seeing an immediate right to vote on the precise law left after cancellation. Historical absence of suits was not conclusive, partly because declaratory relief legislation postdated older examples. He would find standing and affirm on constitutionality. Breyer separately saw concrete impaired legislative work, genuine adversity, and injury at least as serious as Coleman’s isolated incident. He would allow the suit but expressly reserve merits for further argument. The majority neither upheld the Act nor decided that institutional plaintiffs can never sue.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment, qualifications and separate opinions; 521 U.S. 818 n.2, 829–843 & nn.10–11
